title: Building Your Automation Portfolio
summary: In automation, a portfolio of real projects is far more convincing than a list of tools you claim to know, so building and presenting one is what turns your 45 days of learning into job offers and clients. Employers and clients want proof you can sol
content:
# Building Your Automation Portfolio ##### Two candidates, one job A hiring manager at a Bengaluru startup screens two applications for a junior automation role. **Candidate A's résumé** lists: Zapier, Make.com, n8n, Python, APIs, webhooks, JSON, SQL, Docker, OpenAI. Ten technologies, no evidence for any of them. **Candidate B's application** links to a page with three case studies. The first opens: *"A design studio spent 3.5 hours every Friday manually creating 22 invoices, with roughly one error a month reaching a client. I built an automation that generates and emails them from order data. Time dropped to 4 minutes of review; errors went to zero over 90 days of measurement."* Below it: an architecture diagram, the tools used and why, a 3-minute demo video, and a link to the repository. The manager interviews Candidate B. Not because B knows more — they may know less — but because B has **demonstrated** rather than **claimed**. Michael Spence's signalling theory (1973) explains the economics: employers cannot directly observe your ability, so they rely on signals that are *costly to fake*. Anyone can type "Zapier" on a résumé. Only someone who has actually delivered can produce a case study with a measured result. Your portfolio is the highest-quality signal available to you, and today you build it. ##### What an automation portfolio contains Aim for **three to five projects**, presented well. Quality beats quantity decisively — five polished case studies outperform fifteen half-documented ones. Cover a range so you demonstrate breadth: - **The capstone** — your flagship. Multi-system, with a database, AI and monitoring. - **A no-code business automation** — showing you can deliver simple value fast (Zapier/Make). - **A technical build** — Python, an API integration, or self-hosted n8n, showing you are not tool-limited. - **An AI-enabled automation** — classification, extraction or an agent, showing current relevance. - **Optionally a reusable template** published to a community gallery. Each project needs six things: the **problem**, the **solution with an architecture diagram**, the **tools and why you chose them**, a **demo** (video or screenshots), a **measurable result**, and **code or workflow exports** where you can share them. Around the projects, your portfolio also needs a **central page** linking everything, a **GitHub profile** that looks maintained, and a **LinkedIn** that says "automation engineer" rather than "student." ##### The case study structure Use **problem → solution → impact**, always, in that order. ```markdown # Supplier Confirmation Automation *Reduced order confirmation processing by 92% for a logistics SME* ## The problem A logistics company's operations team spent ~22 minutes per purchase order manually reading supplier confirmation emails and re-keying dates, quantities and prices into a tracking sheet — 45 orders a month, roughly 16.5 hours. Manual re-keying caused about 3 errors a month, and 6 missed deliveries a year at ~₹8,000 rework each. Nothing happened at all when the ops lead was on leave. ## What I built An n8n workflow that receives supplier confirmation emails, extracts the fields with an LLM (layout-independent, so supplier template changes don't break it), validates them against the purchase order in PostgreSQL, and either confirms automatically or routes discrepancies to a human with a drafted reply. A 6 p.m. digest replaces the manual WhatsApp summary. [architecture diagram] **Key decisions** - *n8n, self-hosted* — supplier emails contain PII the client required to stay on Indian infrastructure; also gave me a Code node for custom parsing. - *LLM extraction over regex* — 14 suppliers with 14 email formats; regex would break on every template change. - *Confidence threshold + human queue* — extraction is ~93% accurate, so anything uncertain goes to a person rather than being guessed. - *Postgres with a unique key on message ID* — makes duplicate processing structurally impossible, so retries are always safe. **Hardest problem** Forwarded emails arrive without a `Message-ID` header, so a third of my deduplication keys were null. I diagnosed it by comparing raw headers of working and failing runs in the execution log, and fixed it by falling back to a hash of (sender + PO number + date) when the header is absent. ## Impact (measured over 90 days) | Metric | Before | After | |---|---|---| | Time per confirmation | 22 min | 1.8 min | | Ops hours / month | 16.5 | 1.4 | | Re-keying errors / month | ~3 | 0 | | Confirmation lag | ~7 h | 11 min | | Running cost | — | ₹1,050/month | **Net: ~₹1.6 lakh annual value against ₹12,600 annual running cost.** 🎥 [3-minute demo](link) · 💻 [Repository](link) · 📄 [Architecture doc](link) ``` Notice the proportions: the problem gets real space, decisions are justified, one hard problem is described honestly, and impact is numeric. That "hardest problem" paragraph is often what an interviewer asks about first. ##### Why problem–solution–impact beats a tool list The assignment asks you to explain this, and the reasoning is worth being precise about. A tool list answers *"what do you know?"* — a question the employer cannot verify and that everyone answers identically. A case study answers *"what can you do for us?"* and does so with evidence. Specifically it demonstrates four things a list cannot: that you can **identify** a problem worth solving (business judgment); that you can **choose** appropriate tools and defend the choice (engineering judgment); that you can **ship** something that works in reality (execution); and that you can **measure and communicate** value (the thing that makes you promotable). It also gives the interviewer somewhere to go. "Tell me about the discrepancy handling" is a much better conversation than "so, how well do you know Zapier?" ##### Showcasing workflows, diagrams, and demos **Diagrams** do heavy lifting. One Mermaid flowchart communicates an architecture faster than three paragraphs, and Mermaid renders natively on GitHub: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Supplier email] --> B[Verify + dedup] B --> C[LLM extract fields] C --> D{Confidence &
PO match?} D -->|yes| E[(Postgres:
confirm order)] D -->|no| F[Human review
+ Slack] E --> G[6pm digest] F --> G ``` **Demos** are the most under-used asset in junior portfolios. A 2–4 minute Loom recording — problem, live run, one interesting decision, results — converts far better than any amount of text. Keep it short, show real output, and speak plainly. **Workflow exports** prove the work is real. Commit the n8n or Make JSON to the repository (after checking it for secrets), and add screenshots of the canvas. **Sanitize before publishing.** Remove client names if you do not have permission ("a logistics SME in Maharashtra" is fine), scrub real customer data, and re-check every export for credentials. ##### GitHub, a personal site, and templates **GitHub** is your default portfolio host and costs nothing. Structure it as one repository per project with a strong README, plus a profile README (`username/username` repo) that introduces you and links your best three projects. A GitHub profile with recent, meaningful commits is itself a signal of consistency. **A central page** ties it together. Options in ascending order of effort: a Notion page (free, fast, perfectly acceptable), a GitHub Pages site, or a small custom site. Do not let site-building become procrastination — a well-organized Notion page linked from your LinkedIn is entirely sufficient. **Publishing a template** is a strong, low-cost differentiator. n8n's template gallery, Make's template library and Zapier's shared Zaps all accept community submissions. Take a genuinely useful, generalized workflow from your work, strip the client specifics, document it well, and publish it. It demonstrates that other people can use your work — which is exactly what employers are buying — and it generates inbound interest passively. ##### Presenting it everywhere - **LinkedIn** — headline "Automation Engineer | Zapier, Make, n8n, Python, AI Workflows", an About section that tells the story of one project with its result, and Featured links to your case studies. - **Résumé** — projects section before skills, each as one line of impact: *"Built an n8n + PostgreSQL + LLM automation cutting order confirmation time 92% (16.5 → 1.4 ops hours/month)."* - **Cover notes and DMs** — link the single most relevant case study rather than the whole portfolio. - **Content** — writing up one project as a public post regularly generates enquiries; it is the cheapest marketing available. ##### Common pitfalls - **Listing tools instead of showing outcomes.** - **No numbers.** "Improved efficiency" means nothing; "22 min → 1.8 min" means everything. Estimate honestly if you must, and say it is an estimate. - **Tutorial projects** with no real problem behind them. Automate something for a real person, even unpaid. - **Client data left in screenshots or exports.** - **No demo** — video massively outperforms text for automation work. - **Hiding failures.** Describing a hard problem and how you solved it builds more credibility than implying everything went smoothly. - **A dead GitHub** with one commit from eight months ago. - **Perfectionism.** Three good case studies published beat five perfect ones still in draft. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: turn **two projects, including the capstone**, into polished case studies using **problem → solution → impact**, each with a diagram, the tools used, a short demo, and a measurable result — then **publish** them to GitHub or a simple site. Write the problem section first and resist starting with the technology; if the problem does not sound worth solving, the rest will not save it. The mini project is the complete portfolio: a **central page** linking at least **three case studies** with diagrams, demos and results, plus **one reusable template published to a community gallery**. Then do the test that matters — send the link to someone outside your field and ask what you do. If they can explain it back to you, your portfolio works. For the assignment, write **one project as a full case study** and explain in a few sentences why **problem–solution–impact is more persuasive than a tool list**. Use the signalling argument: claims are free and unverifiable, while a measured result is costly to fake and demonstrates business judgment, engineering judgment, delivery and communication all at once. ##### Key takeaways - A portfolio is a costly-to-fake signal; three to five well-documented projects outperform any list of tools. - Structure every case study as problem → solution → impact, with justified decisions and one honestly described hard problem. - Always include a number. Measured before/after results are what convert readers into interviewers. - Diagrams and 2–4 minute demo videos communicate automation work far better than prose — and sanitize every export and screenshot before publishing. - Host on GitHub with a central linking page, publish a community template, and mirror the story on LinkedIn and your résumé.
